newsitem.title: USA: Pittsburgh struggles to shake blue-collar legacy.
newsitem.headline: Pittsburgh struggles to shake blue-collar legacy.

text.p: Westinghouse Electric Corp.'s plan to move its media operations to New York and leave a rump industrial empire in Pittsburgh illustrates the Steel City's struggle to shake its smokestack image and highlight its shift to a white-collar economy, economic experts say.

"It's a metaphor for how people outside Pittsburgh see it," said Lester Lave, economics professor at Carnegie Mellon University's Graduate School of Industrial Administration. "The progressive businesses are going elsewhere, and we're left with the industrial, gritty stuff."

Spurred by its acquisition of CBS Inc., Westinghouse, which has been based in Pittsburgh for more than a century, plans to relocate its media operations to New York and keep its industrial units in Pittsburgh. The groups will be run as separate companies.
Pittsburgh's economy has shifted to white-collar from blue-collar but many outsiders still associate the city with steel mills, iron mines and a population comprised of union workers.

"Many (outsiders) have one of two images of Pittsburgh: a great powerhouse of steelmaking, or what happened after that collapsed, which is a depressed place," said Tim Parks, president of the Pittsburgh Regional Alliance, an economic development group.
"The truth is, we are experiencing a slow but certain rise in the rate of economic growth because of a diversified set of assets."
Development efforts in the public and private sectors have reshaped the region's economy. Several entrepreneurial high-technology firms have started up, offshoots of the city's universities.

One of the best known, Fore Systems Inc., a producer of networking products, was started in 1990 by four members of Carnegie Mellon's computer science department and has grown to some 1,300 employees.

Foreign companies have built manufacturing and research facilities. The Penn Southwest Association, a group charged with attracting new business, was instrumental in bringing a $500 million Sony television manufacturing plant to the region.

Financial service, health care service and biotechnology companies have expanded. The city opened a sprawling, new international airport in 1993. More than $600 million in new construction is planned, including a new baseball stadium.
But the legacy of steel mills lingers, although the city has almost no belching smokestacks and most integrated steel production is in the Midwest.
Namesakes such as the Pittsburgh Steelers and Iron City Beer reinforce Pittsburgh's gritty image, although shops and businesses line riverfronts once dominated by steel mills.

Once the icon of American steelmaking, Pittsburgh lost hundreds of thousands of jobs over the past two decades when unprofitable mills shut down. The city also suffered economic blows from the exodus of some of its corporate giants.
Gulf Oil disappeared when it was bought by Chevron Corp. in 1984. National Steel Corp. moved to Indiana in 1991 to be closer to its steel operations.
Koppers Industries, a huge producer of resins, was broken up under a hostile takeover in 1988 by Beazer Plc, a British company.
The city's population shrunk to about 400,000, commpared with nearly 700,000 in the 1960s.

But the creation of economic development groups that lure investment, along with local government's more cooperative attitude toward business, have made Pittsburgh an area poised for growth, experts said.
Economists said job growth in the Pittsburgh metropolitan area has increased by 1 percent annually since 1993, a rate that lags behind the national average.

"There's no question the pace of growth has been a step behind," said Stuart Hoffman, chief economist at PNC Bank Corp. "But we are riding a rising tide. The pieces are in place for Pittsburgh to better market itself as a place to do business."

Business taxes have been cut during the past few years and the city's budget calls for them to drop further in 1997. Government leaders have been encouraging foreign investment, including from Japanese and Irish companies.

"We still have a lot of work to do in making Pittsburgh a more friendly business climate," said Richard Berner, chief economist at Mellon Bank Corp. "But improvement is out there. I anticipate companies moving here that at first wouldn't have considered it."
